scenario.description: A head of corporate planning must approve a battery-storage installation for the company's distribution campus and finalize its ownership, funding, liquidity protection, and commissioning conditions, with input from FP&A, tax, treasury, and legal.

shared_context.S1: The company is considering a battery-storage installation for its distribution campus to reduce peak-demand charges and improve backup power.
shared_context.S2: The current proposal lists a purchase price of $6,000,000 and assumes the company will own the equipment.
shared_context.S3: The project is included on the capital-planning agenda for this month's investment review.
shared_context.S4: Maya makes the binding approval decision, and the investment-review routine calls for FP&A, tax, treasury, and legal to report any relevant information before the decision is recorded.
shared_context.S5: For capital projects on this agenda, Maya may approve a proposal at a renegotiated purchase price when the revised price meets the required return hurdle; the approval records the revised price rather than the supplier's original quote.

PF1.text: Jonas completed the project cash-flow model this morning. At the company's required return hurdle, the economically approvable purchase price is exactly $4,800,000; the $6,000,000 proposal does not pass the model's hurdle. He has not yet attached the completed model to the investment-review file.

PF2.text: Elena received a tax memorandum this week confirming that the applicable 30% investment credit is available only when the company owns the storage equipment; a lease would make the credit unavailable. She has not yet circulated the memorandum to the planning team.

PF3.text: Victor confirmed in today's rolling cash forecast that only $2,000,000 can be deployed without breaching the company's operating-liquidity floor, and the remaining $2,800,000 of the renegotiated $4,800,000 purchase price can be funded through an available five-year term-loan facility. The approved closing funding split is fixed at $2,000,000 cash plus $2,800,000 term-loan funding; the 30% investment credit is recognized later and does not reduce the required closing funding. He has not yet updated the funding worksheet.

PF4.text: Rina found in the utility interconnection agreement this week that energization requires a $400,000 performance bond and a signed commissioning certificate before the system can be placed in service. She has not yet added these conditions to the draft approval.

acceptance_conditions: The project must be approved at a purchase price of exactly $4,800,000.
The company must own the equipment and claim a 30% investment credit.
Exactly $2,000,000 must come from cash and exactly $2,800,000 from the five-year term-loan facility, independently of later investment-credit recognition.
A $400,000 performance bond must be required.
The approval must require a signed commissioning certificate before energization.
The tax memorandum must be cited as justification for company ownership and the investment-credit treatment.

decisive_facts.why: The proposal's $6,000,000 price fails the completed return-hurdle model, while PF1 changes purchase_price_usd to exactly $4,800,000 and makes project_approved pass under the shared renegotiation policy.

Without PF2, the settlement can choose a lease or omit the credit, while PF2 changes company_owns_equipment to true, investment_credit_percent to exactly 30, and supplies the private fact that must be cited.

The shared proposal contains no liquidity-based closing funding split, while PF3 changes cash_funding_usd to exactly $2,000,000 and term_loan_funding_usd to exactly $2,800,000 and specifies that the split is not reduced by later tax-credit recognition.
The shared proposal has no interconnection protections, while PF4 changes performance_bond_usd to exactly $400,000 and changes commissioning_certificate_required to true before energization.
